items.prompt: What does a fruit develop from in a flower?

options.label: The ovary
options.feedback: Correct. A fruit is the mature ovary of a flower, which enlarges and ripens after pollination.

options.label: The petals
options.feedback: Petals are the colourful parts that attract pollinators; they usually fall off after pollination and do not become the fruit.

options.label: The stamens
options.feedback: Stamens are the male parts that produce pollen; they do not develop into the fruit.

options.label: The stigma
options.feedback: The stigma is the sticky tip that receives pollen; it is part of the female structure but the fruit comes from the ovary below it.

items.ok_line: The fruit grows from the mature ovary.
items.ko_line: Petals and stamens do not form the fruit.
items.exp_text: A fruit is the mature ovary of a flower. After the flower is pollinated, the ovary enlarges and ripens into the fruit that holds the seeds.

items.prompt: Which of these is a simple fruit?

options.label: A raspberry
options.feedback: A raspberry is an aggregate fruit, formed from many ovaries of a single flower, not a simple fruit.

options.label: A pineapple
options.feedback: A pineapple is a multiple fruit, made from the fused ovaries of many flowers, not a simple fruit.

options.label: An apple
options.feedback: Correct. An apple develops from a single ovary, making it a simple fruit, even though its flesh also includes the floral tube.

options.label: A mulberry
options.feedback: A mulberry is a multiple fruit, formed from several flowers that fuse together, not a simple fruit.

items.ok_line: An apple comes from one ovary.
items.ko_line: Aggregate and multiple fruits use more than one ovary.
items.exp_text: A simple fruit forms from a single ovary and may contain one or many seeds. Apples, peaches and tomatoes are simple fruits.

options.label: From several flowers that fuse together
options.feedback: That describes multiple fruits, not aggregate fruits. Aggregate fruits come from a single flower with many ovaries.

options.label: From a single flower with many ovaries
options.feedback: Correct. Aggregate fruits form from one compound flower that contains many separate ovaries, each becoming a small fruitlet.

options.label: From one ovary only
options.feedback: That is a simple fruit, which uses a single ovary, not the many ovaries of an aggregate fruit.

options.label: From the flower's receptacle only
options.feedback: The receptacle is involved in accessory fruits like strawberries, but aggregate fruits come from multiple ovaries in one flower.

items.ok_line: Aggregate fruits use one flower with many ovaries.
items.ko_line: Multiple fruits fuse flowers; aggregate does not.
items.exp_text: An aggregate fruit develops from a single flower that has many separate ovaries. Raspberries and blackberries are examples, each tiny bump being one ovary's fruit.

items.prompt: What type of fruit is a fig?

options.label: A simple fruit
options.feedback: A fig is not a simple fruit; it forms from many flowers, so it belongs to the multiple fruit category.

options.label: An aggregate fruit
options.feedback: Aggregate fruits come from one flower with many ovaries, but a fig is made from the fused ovaries of multiple flowers.

options.label: A drupe
options.feedback: A drupe, like a peach, is a simple fleshy fruit with one seed; a fig is multiple and contains many tiny seeds.

options.label: A multiple fruit
options.feedback: Correct. A fig forms from the fused ovaries of many flowers, making it a multiple fruit, like the mulberry and pineapple.

items.ok_line: A fig comes from many flowers fused together.
items.ko_line: Figs use multiple flowers, not one ovary or one flower.
items.exp_text: A multiple fruit forms when the ovaries of several flowers fuse into one structure. Figs, mulberries and pineapples are multiple fruits.

items.prompt: Which fruit is an example of a pepo?

options.label: A cucumber
options.feedback: Correct. A cucumber is a pepo, a type of berry with an inseparable rind.

options.label: A lemon
options.feedback: A lemon is a hesperidium, which has a separable rind, not a pepo with an inseparable rind.

options.label: An apple
options.feedback: An apple is a pome, where the fleshy part comes from the floral tube and the endocarp is cartilaginous.

options.label: A peach
options.feedback: A peach is a drupe with a single seed and fleshy mesocarp, not a pepo berry.

items.ok_line: Cucumbers are berries with a tough rind.
items.ko_line: Lemon, apple and peach are different categories.
items.exp_text: A pepo is a type of berry with a rind that cannot be separated from the flesh. Cucumbers and melons are pepos.

items.prompt: Which fruit is an example of a hesperidium?

options.label: A cucumber
options.feedback: A cucumber is a pepo with an inseparable rind, not a hesperidium, which has a separable rind.

options.label: A lemon
options.feedback: Correct. A lemon is a hesperidium, a berry with a peel that can be separated from the inner flesh.

options.label: An apple
options.feedback: An apple is a pome, not a hesperidium; its flesh develops from the floral tube rather than the ovary wall alone.

options.label: A peach
options.feedback: A peach is a drupe with a hard stone; it is not a hesperidium berry with a peel.

items.ok_line: Lemons are berries with a removable rind.
items.ko_line: Cucumbers have inseparable rinds, unlike lemons.
items.exp_text: A hesperidium is a type of berry that has a separable rind. Citrus fruits like lemons and oranges are hesperidia.

items.prompt: What makes a strawberry a false fruit?

options.label: It has no seeds at all
options.feedback: Strawberries do have seeds; the tiny specks on the surface are the actual fruits, each with a seed inside.

options.label: It develops from several flowers
options.feedback: Multiple fruits form from several flowers, but a strawberry comes from a single flower; that is not why it is false.

options.label: Its edible flesh comes from the receptacle, not the ovary
options.feedback: Correct. In a strawberry, the fleshy part grows from the flower's receptacle, while the true fruits are the tiny achenes on the surface, so it is called an accessory fruit.

options.label: It is dry instead of fleshy
options.feedback: Strawberries are fleshy fruits, not dry; the false-fruit label comes from which tissue forms the flesh, not from its texture.

items.ok_line: Strawberry flesh comes from the receptacle.
items.ko_line: True fruits use the ovary; strawberries use the receptacle.
items.exp_text: A false fruit, or accessory fruit, is one where the edible part develops from tissues other than the ovary. In strawberries, that tissue is the flower's receptacle.

items.prompt: Which of these is a dry dehiscent fruit?

options.label: A sweet pea pod
options.feedback: Correct. Sweet pea pods are dry dehiscent fruits; they build up internal tension and split open to release seeds.

options.label: A sunflower seed
options.feedback: Sunflower seeds are dry indehiscent fruits; they do not split open but rely on physical forces for dispersal.

options.label: A dandelion
options.feedback: Dandelions are dry indehiscent fruits; they depend on wind and do not burst open to release seeds.

options.label: A walnut
options.feedback: Walnuts are nuts, which are dry indehiscent fruits; they do not open by themselves to release seeds.

items.ok_line: Sweet pea pods split to release seeds.
items.ko_line: Sunflower, dandelion and walnut stay closed.
items.exp_text: Dry dehiscent fruits increase internal tension until the pod bursts open to release seeds. Sweet pea, soybean, milkweed and poppy are examples.

items.prompt: How is the pericarp typically arranged in a fleshy fruit?

options.label: As one single uniform layer
options.feedback: The pericarp in fleshy fruits is not uniform; it has three distinct layers, though they may blend together.

options.label: In two layers only
options.feedback: There are three layers in the pericarp of fleshy fruits, not two: the epicarp, mesocarp and endocarp.

options.label: All layers hard and dry
options.feedback: Hard, dry layers are typical of dry fruits, not fleshy fruits, which have soft, fleshy layers.

options.label: As three layers: epicarp, mesocarp and endocarp
options.feedback: Correct. Fleshy fruits have an outer epicarp, a middle mesocarp and an inner endocarp, though the layers may blend together.

items.ok_line: Fleshy fruits have three pericarp layers.
items.ko_line: The pericarp is made of three distinct layers.
items.exp_text: In fleshy fruits, the pericarp is made of three layers: the outer epicarp, the middle mesocarp and the inner endocarp. These layers vary in thickness and may blend.

items.prompt: What part of the pericarp is the flavedo in citrus fruits?

options.label: The mesocarp
options.feedback: The mesocarp is the middle layer, also called albedo or pith in citrus; the flavedo is the outermost layer.

options.label: The epicarp
options.feedback: Correct. The flavedo is the epicarp, the outermost layer of the pericarp, which forms the coloured skin of citrus fruits.

options.label: The endocarp
options.feedback: The endocarp is the inner layer that surrounds the seeds and forms the segments; the flavedo is the outer skin.

options.label: The seed coat
options.feedback: The seed coat is a layer around the seed itself, not part of the pericarp; the flavedo is part of the fruit's outer wall.

items.ok_line: The flavedo is the citrus outer skin.
items.ko_line: Flavedo sits at the outermost pericarp layer.
items.exp_text: The flavedo is the outermost layer of the pericarp in citrus fruits, commonly called the zest. It contains essential oils and pigments that give the fruit its colour.
